codecs.name: SBC
codecs.owner: Bluetooth SIG (free, required for every Bluetooth headphone)
codecs.summary: The basic codec every Bluetooth headphone and phone must support.
codecs.forYou: If your earbuds cost a few dollars, this is almost certainly what they use. It sounds fine for everyday listening; EQ is the biggest quality upgrade you can give it.
codecs.bitrate: About 328 kbps on Android (up to 452–551 kbps for "SBC XQ" on some custom ROMs)
codecs.earbuds: Every earbud chip, including the cheapest JieLi and Bluetrum chips.
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping. Keep big treble boosts modest: lossy codecs spend more bits on treble.

codecs.name: AAC
codecs.owner: MPEG (licensed; Android uses the Fraunhofer FDK encoder)
codecs.summary: The codec Apple uses, also built into every Android phone.
codecs.forYou: Usually a step up from SBC on cheap earbuds that support it. Android picks it automatically, but a few earbuds are forced back to SBC by Android’s own compatibility list.
codecs.bitrate: Up to about 320 kbps, depending on the earbuds
codecs.phones: Every Android phone (quality varies by phone).
codecs.earbuds: Most earbud chips, including JieLi AC69xx and Bluetrum BT892x.
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping.

codecs.name: aptX
codecs.owner: Qualcomm (encoder free in Android since March 2023)
codecs.summary: Qualcomm’s classic codec with a fixed bitrate.
codecs.forYou: A little more data than SBC. Common on Snapdragon and Samsung phones, rare on very cheap earbuds.
codecs.phones: Snapdragon phones, Google Pixels and Samsung Galaxy phones with Exynos or Snapdragon chips; some MediaTek phones (makers choose).
codecs.earbuds: Mainly Qualcomm QCC chips; rare on JieLi and Bluetrum entry chips.
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping. The bitrate is fixed, so EQ boosts never change it.

codecs.name: aptX HD
codecs.owner: Qualcomm (encoder free in Android since March 2023)
codecs.summary: A 24-bit version of aptX with more data.
codecs.forYou: Slightly more detail than aptX when both phone and earbuds support it. Samsung Galaxy phones do not.
codecs.bitrate: 576 kbps at 48 kHz (529 kbps at 44.1 kHz)
codecs.phones: Many Snapdragon phones (e.g. Xiaomi 15); reported on Pixel; not on Samsung Galaxy.
codecs.earbuds: Qualcomm QCC chips and a few headphones.
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping.

codecs.name: aptX Low Latency
codecs.summary: A low-delay aptX variant used by USB and optical transmitters.
codecs.forYou: No Android phone can send it. For gaming, use your earbuds’ game mode, LE Audio, LLAC or aptX Adaptive’s low-latency mode instead.
codecs.earbuds: Older Qualcomm QCC30xx-class headsets and transmitter dongles.

codecs.name: aptX Adaptive
codecs.summary: Qualcomm’s codec that changes its bitrate with radio conditions, with a low-latency mode.
codecs.forYou: Great when it works, but it only exists on Snapdragon phones whose maker turned it on. MediaTek, Google Pixel and Samsung Galaxy phones cannot use it, whatever the earbuds support. Quality can dip when the signal is weak.
codecs.audio: 16 or 24-bit, 44.1/48 kHz (96 kHz on some hardware)
codecs.latency: About 80 ms system latency, plus a low-latency mode (Qualcomm)
codecs.phones: Snapdragon 855 and newer when the maker enables it (Xiaomi 15, Honor Magic/GT/number series, Motorola, vivo, OnePlus Snapdragon models).
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping. Android does not report this codec by a standard number, so the badge may say "vendor codec".

codecs.name: aptX Lossless (Snapdragon Sound)
codecs.summary: CD-quality lossless Bluetooth for certified Snapdragon phones and earbuds.
codecs.forYou: Only with a certified Snapdragon phone and matching earbuds. EQ still works: the lossless link simply carries the EQ’d sound faithfully.
codecs.bitrate: About 1.1–1.2 Mbps for 16-bit/44.1 kHz, scaling down to about 140 kbps; newer chips up to 2.1 Mbps at 24-bit/48 kHz
codecs.audio: 16-bit/44.1 kHz, or 24-bit/48 kHz on newer platforms
codecs.phones: Certified Snapdragon phones (Xiaomi, vivo, Motorola and others).
codecs.earbuds: Qualcomm QCC5171, QCC3071 (16/44.1), QCC3091 (24/48), S3/S5 Gen 3, S7 family.
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping.

codecs.name: LDAC
codecs.summary: Sony’s high-bitrate codec with three quality levels.
codecs.forYou: The best widely available codec on Android when your earbuds support it. "Best effort" (ABR) mode can drop to low bitrates and stutter; a fixed 660 kbps is usually the most stable choice, 990 kbps if the signal is clean.
codecs.bitrate: 330 / 660 / 990 kbps at 48/96 kHz (303 / 606 / 909 kbps at 44.1/88.2 kHz); adaptive mode steps between them
codecs.latency: About 320 ms averaged over four flagship phones, close to SBC and aptX (second-hand measurement)
codecs.phones: Nearly every Android 8+ phone, including Samsung, Pixel, Xiaomi (also MediaTek models), OPPO, vivo, Honor and Huawei.
codecs.earbuds: Sony (e.g. WF-1000XM6), Bluetrum BT891x/892x/897x, JieLi JL7018 (FiiO EH11) and some BES and Airoha designs (not confirmed per chip). Not Galaxy Buds4.
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping. At 96 kHz the filters are recalculated for the higher sample rate.

codecs.name: LHDC (v3/v4/v5, Lossless, LHDC-V)
codecs.owner: Savitech (with Huawei in the HWA Union; licensed)
codecs.summary: A high-resolution codec popular with Chinese phone and earbud makers.
codecs.forYou: High quality when both sides support it, mostly on Xiaomi, OPPO, vivo, Honor, Huawei and (since Android 17) Pixel 9 Pro and newer. Samsung phones do not support it.
codecs.bitrate: 160–1000 kbps (v5 about 1 Mbps); LHDC Lossless 1–1.4 Mbps
codecs.audio: Up to 24-bit/192 kHz on paper; 96 kHz on Pixel
codecs.phones: Xiaomi (incl. MediaTek models), Honor (MagicOS 10: LHDC 5.0), OPPO/OnePlus/realme, vivo, Motorola, Huawei, Pixel 9 Pro+ on Android 17.
codecs.earbuds: BES2500Y (OPPO Enco X), reportedly BES2600/2700 (Moto Buds), Bluetrum BT892x/897x, vivo TWS 5 Hi-Fi, some Nothing/OnePlus/Edifier models.
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping. Hi-res sample rates mean the filters are recalculated per rate.

codecs.name: LLAC (LHDC Low Latency)
codecs.summary: A low-latency version of LHDC for gaming.
codecs.forYou: Good for games on phones and earbuds that both support it (mostly Huawei and some Chinese gaming earbuds).
codecs.phones: Huawei (since P30) and some Chinese phones paired with gaming earbuds.
codecs.eqNote: The in-app player adds no delay. System-wide, FreeEQ adds a short processing delay: about 20 ms with Precision on "Best for video", which Automatic picks for games.

codecs.name: LC3 (LE Audio) and Auracast
codecs.summary: The new LE Audio codec: efficient, low-latency, and the basis of Auracast sharing.
codecs.forYou: Newer phones and earbuds use it for LE Audio, which can cut delay and save battery. Android shows FreeEQ that LE Audio is active, but the detailed settings stay hidden unless you use the optional Shizuku mode.
codecs.audio: Usually up to 48 kHz; 7.5 or 10 ms frames
codecs.latency: Lower than classic Bluetooth (under 50 ms in theory)
codecs.phones: Pixel 7 and newer (Auracast on Pixel 8+, not 8a/9a), Samsung One UI 5.1+/7, Xiaomi 14T Pro and 15, most 2024+ flagships.
codecs.earbuds: Galaxy Buds4, Sony WF/WH-XM6, Airoha AB1565/1568/1585, Qualcomm QCC3071+/5171+/3091, Bluetrum BT897x, Realtek RTL8763E/8773E. Not entry JieLi/Bluetrum chips.
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping. Lower bitrate per channel means headroom matters even more.

codecs.name: LC3plus
codecs.summary: An extended LC3 with high-resolution and ultra-low-delay modes.
codecs.forYou: No mainstream Android phone offers it today; if it ever shows up, FreeEQ will show it as a vendor codec.
codecs.bitrate: Varies; high-resolution mode up to 96 kHz/24-bit
codecs.latency: Down to about 7 ms in ultra-low-delay mode
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping.

codecs.name: Opus (Pixel Buds)
codecs.owner: IETF codec, used by Google as a Bluetooth vendor codec
codecs.summary: Google’s codec for Pixel phones with Pixel Buds Pro.
codecs.forYou: If you have a Pixel and Pixel Buds Pro, this is normal. Other phones do not turn it on.
codecs.latency: Not published (it uses 10 or 20 ms frames)
codecs.phones: Pixel phones with Pixel Buds Pro.
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping.

codecs.name: Samsung Seamless / Scalable Codec (SSC, SSC HiFi, SSC UHQ)
codecs.summary: Samsung’s own codec between Galaxy phones and Galaxy Buds.
codecs.forYou: Only works with a Galaxy phone and Galaxy Buds. UHQ (24-bit/96 kHz) needs the "Ultra High Quality Audio" setting. Samsung’s own sound settings can stack with FreeEQ, so keep them neutral.
codecs.bitrate: Adaptive; SSC HiFi reported at 584 kbps (sources conflict)
codecs.audio: SSC HiFi 24-bit/48 kHz; SSC UHQ 24-bit/96 kHz
codecs.phones: Samsung Galaxy phones and tablets (Exynos and Snapdragon).
codecs.earbuds: Galaxy Buds2 Pro (HiFi), Buds3 Pro and Buds4 Pro (UHQ).
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping. It appears as a vendor codec.

codecs.name: Huawei L2HC
codecs.summary: Huawei’s high-resolution codec for FreeBuds on Huawei phones.
codecs.forYou: Only between Huawei phones and Huawei FreeBuds; FreeEQ shows it as a vendor codec if it appears.
codecs.bitrate: L2HC 3.0: 64–1920 kbps; L2HC 4.0: up to 2.3 Mbps
codecs.phones: Huawei phones on EMUI/HarmonyOS (L2HC 4.0 needs EMUI 15+).
codecs.eqNote: FreeEQ works before the phone compresses the sound for Bluetooth, so it always keeps some headroom (a negative preamp and a limiter) to stop boosts from clipping.

ldacModes.name: Quality (990 kbps)
ldacModes.advice: Best sound; needs a clean signal close to the phone.

ldacModes.name: Standard (660 kbps)
ldacModes.advice: The most stable choice for most people.

ldacModes.name: Connection (330 kbps)
ldacModes.advice: Survives a weak signal but sounds no better than AAC.

ldacModes.name: Best effort (adaptive)
ldacModes.advice: Can drop quality or stutter; pick 660 kbps if you hear dropouts.

phoneChips.name: Qualcomm Snapdragon
phoneChips.advice: Snapdragon phones have the widest codec choice. aptX Adaptive and aptX Lossless work only if your phone maker enabled them and your earbuds have a Qualcomm chip.
notes: aptX Adaptive needs Snapdragon 855 or newer and the maker’s support; Android does not report it by a standard number.
aptX Lossless needs a Snapdragon Sound certified phone and earbuds.
LC3 (LE Audio) needs Android 13 or newer and a phone whose maker turned it on; most 2024 and newer flagships have it.
Samsung Galaxy phones with Snapdragon use Samsung’s codec set instead (see the Samsung entry).
examples: Xiaomi 15 (SBC, AAC, aptX, aptX HD, aptX Adaptive, LDAC, LHDC 1.0–5.0, LC3)

phoneChips.name: MediaTek Dimensity / Helio
phoneChips.advice: Your MediaTek phone can’t do aptX Adaptive or aptX Lossless, even if your earbuds can. LDAC (660 kbps is the stable setting) is your best option, or LHDC if your phone offers it.
notes: realme confirms MediaTek models cannot select aptX Adaptive "due to the limitations of the MTK processor platform".
Some makers leave out aptX entirely: the Xiaomi 14T Pro lists AAC, LDAC, LHDC 4.0 and LC3 only.
vivo worked with MediaTek to bring LHDC lossless (up to 1.4 Mbps) to Dimensity phones.
LHDC and LC3 (LE Audio) are on Dimensity phones whose makers ship them, such as the Xiaomi 14T Pro; budget Helio phones often have neither.

On Samsung Galaxy A models with MediaTek chips, Samsung picks the codecs. Its Exynos and Snapdragon Galaxies get SBC, AAC, aptX, LDAC and Samsung’s own codec (SSC), but nobody has published the list for the MediaTek models, so trust the codecs your phone reports.
examples: Samsung Galaxy A models with MediaTek chips

phoneChips.name: Samsung Galaxy
phoneChips.advice: On Galaxy phones with Exynos or Snapdragon chips, Samsung decides the codecs, not the chip: SBC, AAC, aptX, LDAC and Samsung’s own codec (SSC) with Galaxy Buds, but not aptX HD, aptX Adaptive or LHDC, even on Snapdragon models.
notes: Samsung’s press claim that the Galaxy S25 adds aptX HD/Adaptive and LHDC was corrected: it has the same codecs as earlier models.
SSC UHQ (24-bit/96 kHz) needs Galaxy Buds3 Pro or Buds4 Pro and the "Ultra High Quality Audio" setting.
LE Audio (LC3) arrived with One UI 5.1 and Auracast with One UI 7, on models whose hardware supports it.
This codec set is confirmed for Exynos and Snapdragon Galaxies only. Galaxy A models with MediaTek or Unisoc chips are listed under those chips, because nobody has published their exact list.
Exynos phones from other makers follow that maker’s codec list, not Samsung’s.
examples: Galaxy A models with Exynos or Snapdragon chips

phoneChips.name: Google Pixel
phoneChips.advice: Pixels support LDAC, Opus with Pixel Buds Pro and, from Pixel 7, LC3 (LE Audio); Android 17 added LHDC v5 on Pixel 9 Pro and newer. aptX Adaptive is not available.
notes: LHDC v5 (up to 96 kHz) appears under Developer options > Bluetooth audio codec only while an LHDC v5 headset is connected.
LE Audio arrived with Pixel 7 / Android 13; Auracast audio sharing with Android 16 QPR1 on Pixel 8 and newer (not 8a/9a).
Reports about aptX and aptX HD on the Pixel 9 versus the 9a conflict.

phoneChips.name: Unisoc (budget phones)
phoneChips.advice: On budget Unisoc phones, expect SBC or AAC. EQ is the biggest improvement you can make.
notes: The exact codec list of Unisoc phones is not documented publicly; it likely follows standard Android (SBC, AAC, maybe LDAC and aptX).
This includes budget Samsung Galaxy A0x models: Samsung has not published which codecs they get.
examples: Budget Samsung A0x, Tecno, Infinix, Nokia and ZTE models

phoneChips.name: Huawei Kirin
phoneChips.advice: Huawei phones support LDAC, LHDC and, with Huawei FreeBuds, L2HC. Phones on HarmonyOS NEXT cannot run Android apps like FreeEQ.
notes: L2HC 4.0 needs EMUI 15 or newer.
LLAC (low-latency LHDC) has been on Huawei phones since the P30.
examples: Huawei Mate, Pura and nova series

earbudChips.name: JieLi
earbudChips.foundIn: The largest share of no-name $1–$15 wireless earbuds (about 26% of all TWS main chips in 2022).
earbudChips.codecs: SBC and AAC (mSBC for calls). The JL7018 appears with LDAC in the FiiO EH11, although its datasheet lists SBC/AAC.
earbudChips.forYou: Expect SBC (maybe AAC) and roughly 150–200 ms of delay. There is no hi-res option, so EQ is the one real quality lever.
notes: JieLi holds a patent on online earphone EQ tuning; many buds have onboard EQ modes that change the sound.

earbudChips.name: Bluetrum
earbudChips.foundIn: The second-largest white-label TWS chip maker (about 20% in 2022), historically the cheapest chips.
earbudChips.codecs: Entry AB573x: no hi-res codec. BT891x: LDAC. BT892x: AAC, LHDC, LDAC. BT897x: LE Audio plus LDAC/LHDC.
earbudChips.forYou: Many of these chips have a built-in "bass enhancement" engine. Turn off the earbuds’ own bass or EQ mode first ("flatten your buds"), then let FreeEQ correct them.
notes: BT892x: about 120 ms delay normally, under 65 ms in game mode. Game mode lives in the earbud firmware.

earbudChips.name: Bestechnic (BES)
earbudChips.foundIn: Mid-range buds from Huawei, Xiaomi/Redmi, OPPO, Motorola and similar brands ($20–$200).
earbudChips.codecs: LHDC on BES2500Y (OPPO Enco X) and reportedly BES2600/2700 (Moto Buds). BES2800 codec list unconfirmed.
earbudChips.forYou: Often offers an LHDC or LDAC option next to SBC/AAC; check your earbuds’ app.
notes: BES2700YP is in Huawei FreeBuds Pro 2; BES2700IHC is in Redmi Buds 6.

earbudChips.name: Airoha
earbudChips.foundIn: Mid-tier brands, and some white-label earbuds.
earbudChips.codecs: LE Audio on AB1565/AB1568/AB1585. LDAC is not confirmed by any datasheet found.
earbudChips.forYou: Probably SBC, AAC and LC3; some designs add LDAC.
notes: AB1585 has a HiFi 5 DSP; AB1595 is the AI flagship (late 2024).

earbudChips.name: Realtek
earbudChips.foundIn: Budget to mid-range earbuds (teardown reports name SoundPeats/QCY-class models; unverified per model).
earbudChips.codecs: RTL8763E/RTL8773E: dual-mode classic Bluetooth plus LE Audio.
earbudChips.forYou: Treat as SBC/AAC, plus LC3 on newer parts, unless your phone reports otherwise.

earbudChips.name: Actions
earbudChips.foundIn: Smartwatches and some budget audio products.
earbudChips.codecs: ATS308x: watch chip with LE Audio. ATS296X: announced Bluetooth HDT support.
earbudChips.forYou: Treat as SBC/AAC (plus LC3 on newer parts) unless your phone reports otherwise.

earbudChips.name: Qualcomm QCC
earbudChips.foundIn: Mid and premium earbuds (Jabra, Nothing, Bose, Xiaomi Buds 5 Pro, older Sony). Usually $40 and up.
earbudChips.codecs: aptX, aptX HD and aptX Adaptive (QCC304x and newer); aptX Lossless (QCC5171/3071/3091); LE Audio (QCC3071 and newer); Wi-Fi audio (QCC7226).
earbudChips.forYou: With a Snapdragon phone you may get aptX Adaptive or Lossless; with other phones it falls back to AAC, SBC or LDAC.
notes: The Qualcomm GAIA service UUID 00001107-D102-11E1-9B23-00025B00A5A5 is believed to identify QCC/CSR earbuds (unverified).

effects.name: Dolby Atmos (Dolby Audio Processing)

uuids.note: Classic Dolby DAP type (Samsung, Motorola, Xiaomi direct DAP)

effects.whatItDoes: Adds its own EQ ("intelligent EQ"), volume leveller and virtual surround on top of everything. It is the most common reason a correction sounds wrong.
effects.howToTurnOff: Turn Dolby Atmos off (often a quick-settings tile or Settings > Sound), or set it to "Music" with intelligent EQ off.
effects.foundOn: Samsung, Xiaomi/Redmi/POCO, Motorola, OnePlus, Sony, Nokia, Tecno, Lenovo, Razer and others.

effects.name: Dolby game, voice and spatial helpers
effects.whatItDoes: Game and voice processing, a music volume listener and the spatial-audio renderer that ship alongside Dolby Atmos.
effects.howToTurnOff: Turn off Dolby Atmos and spatial audio for headphones in Sound settings.
effects.foundOn: Xiaomi, Samsung and MediaTek Redmi phones.

effects.name: Dirac
effects.whatItDoes: Applies its own headphone tuning to everything, which stacks with FreeEQ.
effects.howToTurnOff: Look for Dirac or "sound effects" in Sound settings (on Xiaomi: the Earphones / sound effects page) and turn it off.
effects.foundOn: Older Xiaomi phones, Nothing Phone (1), OnePlus 7–9 era, some realme/vivo.

effects.name: DTS (DTS:X Ultra, DTS Headphone:X, DTS Sound)
effects.whatItDoes: Attaches itself to every music stream, in the same effect chain as FreeEQ, so its sound stacks with FreeEQ’s.
effects.howToTurnOff: Turn DTS off in Sound settings (look for "DTS" or "Sound effects").
effects.foundOn: Infinix Zero Ultra, Asus Zenfone 5/6, ZTE/nubia.

effects.name: Samsung SoundAlive (Equalizer)
effects.whatItDoes: Powers One UI’s built-in equalizer and sound presets.
effects.howToTurnOff: Settings > Sounds and vibration > Sound quality and effects: set Equalizer to "Normal".

effects.name: Samsung MySpace (sa3d)
effects.whatItDoes: Attached to music, ringtone and alarm streams on Galaxy phones, in the same chain as FreeEQ.
effects.howToTurnOff: Keep Samsung’s sound effects (Dolby Atmos, Equalizer, Adapt Sound) off or neutral.
effects.foundOn: Galaxy S22 and S24 (configs verified), likely most One UI phones.

effects.name: Samsung SoundBooster+ and volume monitor
effects.whatItDoes: Loudness and volume-monitoring helpers used by One UI.
effects.howToTurnOff: Nothing to do; shown for completeness.

effects.name: Xiaomi Mi Sound
effects.whatItDoes: Headphone-model presets and a personal sound profile that stack with FreeEQ.
effects.howToTurnOff: Open Sound settings > Earphones (sound effects): turn off the headphone-type preset and personalised sound.
effects.foundOn: Xiaomi, Redmi and POCO phones (MIUI / HyperOS).

effects.name: Sony sound enhancement (ClearAudio+, EQ)
effects.whatItDoes: Xperia’s own equalizer and enhancement presets.
effects.howToTurnOff: Settings > Sound & vibration > Playback quality > Audio effect: switch effects off.

effects.name: Sony 360 Reality Audio Upmix
effects.whatItDoes: Turns stereo into virtual surround in compatible apps, which changes the tonal balance.
effects.howToTurnOff: Settings > Sound & vibration > Playback quality > Audio effect: turn off 360 Upmix.

effects.name: OReality Audio
effects.whatItDoes: The phone maker’s sound enhancement, applied to everything you play.
effects.howToTurnOff: Turn off OReality Audio (or the phone’s "sound effects") in Sound settings.
effects.foundOn: realme (e.g. GT 6T), OPPO and OnePlus phones.

effects.name: Waves MaxxAudio (Moto Waves)
effects.whatItDoes: A global enhancement engine with its own EQ.
effects.howToTurnOff: Turn off Moto Audio / Waves in Sound settings.
effects.foundOn: Motorola (Moto G and Edge), older vivo, some LG.

effects.name: Motorola audio effects (mmieffects)
effects.whatItDoes: Motorola’s own effect wrapper, shipped next to Dolby.
effects.howToTurnOff: Turn off Dolby Atmos / Moto Audio in Sound settings.

effects.name: vivo sound effects (vafx, BBE)
effects.whatItDoes: vivo’s Hi-Fi and headphone effects, applied to everything.
effects.howToTurnOff: Turn off vivo’s Hi-Fi / sound effects in Sound settings.
effects.foundOn: vivo and iQOO phones (Funtouch OS / OriginOS).

effects.name: Meizu Square Sound
effects.whatItDoes: Meizu’s equalizer, bass boost and virtualizer.
effects.howToTurnOff: Turn off Meizu’s sound effects in Sound settings.

effects.name: Arkamys
effects.whatItDoes: A licensed sound enhancement engine.
effects.howToTurnOff: Turn off the phone’s sound effects in Sound settings.

effects.name: ICEpower
effects.whatItDoes: A licensed sound enhancement engine.
effects.howToTurnOff: Turn off the phone’s sound effects in Sound settings.

effects.name: AM3D
effects.whatItDoes: A licensed 3D / enhancement engine.
effects.howToTurnOff: Turn off the phone’s sound effects in Sound settings.

effects.name: ViPER4Android
effects.whatItDoes: A root-installed audio mod with its own EQ and effects.
effects.howToTurnOff: Disable ViPER4Android’s processing (or its module) while using FreeEQ.

effects.name: JamesDSP
effects.whatItDoes: A root-installed audio mod with its own EQ and effects.
effects.howToTurnOff: Disable JamesDSP’s processing while using FreeEQ.

effects.name: Qualcomm offload effects (bass boost, virtualizer, EQ)
effects.whatItDoes: Standard Android effects (used by built-in "MusicFX"-style equalizers) that can run on the Snapdragon DSP. They only do something when an app turns them on.
effects.howToTurnOff: Make sure no other equalizer app or built-in equalizer is switched on.
effects.foundOn: Snapdragon phones (Xiaomi, Motorola, Sony, OnePlus and others).

effects.name: Qualcomm audiosphere, shoebox and volume listeners
effects.whatItDoes: Helpers that ride along with music playback. The volume listener may be why the old "global" equalizer mode does nothing on some Snapdragon phones (an inference, not confirmed).
effects.howToTurnOff: Nothing to do; if the global mode fails, FreeEQ’s per-app mode still works.

effects.name: Android DynamicsProcessing
effects.whatItDoes: Android’s built-in multi-band EQ engine. FreeEQ uses it, and so do other EQ apps (Wavelet, Poweramp Equalizer); two apps on the same audio share one engine and only one controls it.
effects.howToTurnOff: If another EQ app keeps taking over, close or uninstall it so FreeEQ can keep control.

oems.name: Google Pixel
works: Per-app mode works with players that announce themselves (Spotify, YouTube Music and others).
No Dolby- or Dirac-style music engine: the cleanest base for correction.
conflicts: Spatial Audio changes the sound with a head model and limits which audio the global mode reaches.
Global mode: LDAC and aptX streams skipped the global effect on Pixel 6/7/8a while SBC and AAC worked; on a Pixel 10a with Android 17 global mode had no effect at all.
Adaptive Sound only tunes the phone speaker, not headphones.
steps: Open your earbuds’ Bluetooth settings and turn off Spatial Audio / head tracking for the most accurate sound.
Close or uninstall other equalizer apps (only one app can control the EQ at a time).
unlockSteps: Android 17 broke app detection on some Pixels (7 Pro, 8a): the player’s audio was found but no EQ was attached (Wavelet reports). If a player stays unprocessed after the unlock, play your music in FreeEQ’s own player.

oems.name: Samsung Galaxy
works: Per-app mode works; global mode worked on a Galaxy S23 Ultra.
On Galaxy phones with Exynos or Snapdragon chips, Galaxy Buds can use Samsung’s own codec (SSC).
conflicts: Dolby Atmos, the One UI Equalizer and Adapt Sound all add their own EQ on top of FreeEQ.
The UHQ upscaler can cause clipping with third-party EQ (one developer’s report).
With Galaxy Buds connected, 360 Audio replaces the Dolby Atmos menu.
A user reported the built-in equalizer stopped working once another EQ app was installed.
steps: Turn off Dolby Atmos (quick-settings tile or Sound quality and effects).
Set the Equalizer to Normal.
Turn off Adapt Sound.
If you hear crackling, set UHQ upscaler to "Bit upscaling only".
Turn off 360 Audio for Galaxy Buds.
Remove Sound Assistant’s equalizer if you use it.

oems.name: Xiaomi, Redmi and POCO
works: Per-app mode works; the global mode worked on a Xiaomi 17 Ultra and a Redmi Note 13.
conflicts: Dolby Atmos (newer models), Mi Sound headphone presets and Dirac (older models) stack with FreeEQ.
MediaTek-based models may also run MediaTek’s loudness processing inside the audio hardware layer, which no app can switch off.
One HyperOS build for the POCO F7 (OS3.0.5.0.WOJMIXM) had a Dolby audio bug and was pulled (third-party report).
steps: Turn off Dolby Atmos.
Open Sound settings > Earphones and turn off the headphone-type preset and personalised sound.
Close or uninstall other equalizer apps (only one app can control the EQ at a time).
unlockSteps: In Developer options, also turn on "USB debugging (Security settings)" before the one-time unlock.

oems.name: OnePlus, OPPO and realme
conflicts: Dolby Atmos (e.g. OnePlus 9 Pro), OReality Audio (e.g. realme GT 6T) or Dirac (older OnePlus) stack with FreeEQ.
realme phones with MediaTek chips cannot use aptX Adaptive.
steps: Turn off Dolby Atmos, OReality Audio or other sound effects in Sound settings.
Close or uninstall other equalizer apps (only one app can control the EQ at a time).
unlockSteps: OPPO and realme: turn off "permission monitoring" in the security centre before the one-time unlock.
OnePlus: turn on "Disable permission monitoring" in Developer options before the one-time unlock.

oems.name: vivo and iQOO
conflicts: vivo’s Hi-Fi and headphone effects (and Waves on older models) stack with FreeEQ.
steps: Turn off vivo’s Hi-Fi / sound effects in Sound settings.
Close or uninstall other equalizer apps (only one app can control the EQ at a time).

oems.name: Motorola
conflicts: Dolby Atmos (e.g. Edge 30 Ultra) or Moto Waves / Moto Audio stack with FreeEQ.
steps: Turn off Dolby Atmos or Moto Audio in Sound settings.
Close or uninstall other equalizer apps (only one app can control the EQ at a time).

oems.name: Sony Xperia
conflicts: Xperia’s audio effects (ClearAudio+/EQ, Dolby Sound, 360 Upmix) change the sound on top of FreeEQ.
DSEE adds high-frequency detail after FreeEQ inside Sony’s audio hardware layer.
steps: Settings > Sound & vibration > Playback quality > Audio effect: turn the effects off (including DSEE and 360 Upmix).
Close or uninstall other equalizer apps (only one app can control the EQ at a time).

oems.name: Nothing and CMF
conflicts: The Nothing Phone (1) ships a Dirac engine that processes everything.
steps: If Sound settings offer Dirac or another sound effect, turn it off.
Close or uninstall other equalizer apps (only one app can control the EQ at a time).

oems.name: Tecno, Infinix and itel
conflicts: DTS (e.g. Infinix Zero Ultra) or Dolby Atmos (e.g. Tecno Pova 6 Pro) stack with FreeEQ.
MediaTek-based models may also run MediaTek’s loudness processing in the audio hardware layer, which no app can change.
steps: Turn off DTS or Dolby Atmos in Sound settings.
Close or uninstall other equalizer apps (only one app can control the EQ at a time).

oems.name: Huawei and Honor
works: Per-app mode works on Android-based EMUI and MagicOS phones.
Honor’s Snapdragon lines support aptX Adaptive; MagicOS 10 adds LHDC 5.0.
conflicts: Huawei Histen effects apply to wired headphones only.
On a Honor MagicPad 4 the global mode worked on the speaker but not over Bluetooth.
Phones on HarmonyOS NEXT (5.x) cannot run Android apps, including FreeEQ.
Spotify 9.1.12 on one Honor phone (Android 16) did not apply system effects (user report).
steps: Wired headphones on Huawei: Settings > Sounds & vibration > Huawei Histen sound effects, choose Natural/Fidelity (or Standard).
Use FreeEQ’s per-app mode for Bluetooth.
Close or uninstall other equalizer apps (only one app can control the EQ at a time).

oems.name: Other phones
works: Per-app mode works with players that announce themselves; the global mode depends on the phone and is checked by a listening test.
conflicts: Any built-in "sound effects", Dolby or spatial audio stacks with FreeEQ.
Hi-res "direct" output, USB DAC bit-perfect mode, Dolby Atmos passthrough and low-latency game audio bypass every app EQ.
If the global mode does nothing over Bluetooth, the Developer option "Disable Bluetooth A2DP hardware offload" may be on.
steps: Turn off the phone’s own sound effects, Dolby or equalizer.
Open your earbuds’ Bluetooth settings and turn off Spatial Audio / head tracking for the most accurate sound.
If you hear no difference over Bluetooth or a USB DAC, try setting the Bluetooth sample rate to 48 kHz or the codec to SBC in Developer options.
In music players with a hi-res or bit-perfect output option, switch it off (e.g. VLC: Audio output = AudioTrack).
Close or uninstall other equalizer apps (only one app can control the EQ at a time).

players.name: Spotify
players.notes: One user report: Spotify 9.1.12 on a Honor phone with Android 16 did not apply system effects.

players.name: Poweramp
players.setting: Settings > Audio engine > Advanced tweaks > MusicFX: turn on.
players.notes: If Poweramp’s Hi-Res output is on, the EQ can be bypassed; turn it off.

players.name: BlackPlayer
players.setting: Turn on BlackPlayer’s equalizer option in its settings (listed as required by Wavelet’s guide; the menu name can vary by version).

players.name: VLC
players.setting: In VLC’s audio settings, set "Audio output" to AudioTrack.

players.name: TIDAL
players.notes: Works with the unlock in other EQ apps; one Android 17 report saw TIDAL’s audio detected but not processed.

players.name: Apple Music
players.notes: Announces itself only sometimes ("very buggy"). Dolby Atmos spatial tracks bypass app EQ; lossless stereo tracks do not.

players.name: YouTube
players.notes: One article says YouTube hides its audio from detection; other EQ apps report it working after the unlock.

players.name: Most preinstalled music players
players.notes: Samsung Music is a notable exception and works out of the box.

playerSupport.works: Works out of the box: the player tells Android when it starts playing, so FreeEQ attaches automatically.
playerSupport.needs-setting: Works after you switch on one setting inside the player.
playerSupport.needs-unlock: The player never announces itself. FreeEQ reaches it after the one-time unlock (or through the global mode on phones where it works).
